en: From the *Lengyan Jujing Shi Chan* (The Ultimate Repentance Ritual of the Śūraṅgama), Volume One:
In performing the ultimate repentance ritual of the Śūraṅgama, it is unnecessary to perform separate Buddhist rites; there is no need to submit petitions or official documents;
gold, silver, money, or cloth offerings are not required; and one need not strike the *nāga-ghaṇṭā*, *kettledrums*, or *cloud-cymbals*. One should simply invite renowned monks.
Virtuous person, chant the text of repentance aloud, contemplate the nature of sin with stillness, visualize the image of the Buddha, and perform prostrations with utmost sincerity;

you will surely achieve a spiritual response. Just as the moon appears when the water is clear and an image arises when the mirror is polished, if you maintain mindfulness within yourself, there shall be nothing that does not accord with your wishes. First, arrange the offerings according to your means.
Images of the Buddha, images of Bodhisattvas, images of Arhats, and images of the various devas who protect the Dharma;
pure water and pure tea; a pure mirror; famous incense; lamps and candles; seasonal flowers, seasonal fruits, and seasonal melons;
rice of the three virtues; vegetables of the six flavors; and all the rare treasures contained within the chamber.
Use precious, exquisite, fresh, and clean fabrics and silks; all must be arranged for offering. One must not conceal the fine with the coarse, nor hide the new by using the worn-out.
First, recite the Great Buddha-Top Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī to establish the boundary; next, solemnly prepare the offerings and offer praises.
Next, the method for opening the rite of repentance:

The first scroll begins with the formal invocation of the rite of repentance, [reflecting that] the mundane world rolls on and the ocean of karma is vast and boundless. At the very beginning, one was unaware; suddenly, ignorance arose. From that point on...
The Dharma-realm flows in divergent streams until, following conditions, it is submerged in tears; rushing toward objects, each part remains unaware of the others.

The realms undergo formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness; the mind undergoes arising, abiding, change, and cessation. Enveloped by the five aggregates, one indulges recklessly in the five desires.
Thoughts and anxieties drift and vanish like motes of dust in the air; actions and movements are frivolous and wild like waves upon the sea. Thus, it comes to pass that...
Phenomena arise dependent upon the mind; as one perceives objects, emotions are born. Thus, the cycle of the six realms turns without ceasing, and the forms of the seven destinies are boundless.

Whether empty, scattered, dissipated, or submerged, all possess the virtuous marks of the Tathāgata. Even the crawling insects and the flying creatures alike receive the spiritual awareness of the Sugata.
The celestial palaces abound in pleasure, yet human birth is difficult to attain—like casting a mustard seed through the eye of a needle. Among these states, the winds and rains are most [intense].

How arduous! A tortoise encounters a drifting raft; at this juncture, the turbulent waves are not easily crossed. Although the three causes and three conditions are already complete, the seven-times-seven and ten-month periods are rarely fulfilled.
Suffering myriad forms while dwelling in and emerging from the womb; undergoing various ailments throughout the three stages and nine years.
Once the union of husband and wife exists, one is burdened by the cares of sons and daughters, causing the mind’s threads to fly in disarray.
This toiling physical form clings to the self and indulges in others; it loves the beautiful and hates the loathsome, deeply stained by worldly dharmas as if glued together like lacquer and resin.
Sentimental desires entwine like fish and water, while one hastens toward the times and seeks out perilous paths, harming others to preserve oneself.
For profit, they slaughter livestock and purchase meat with money; they know only to nourish their own mouths and bodies, yet fail to consider that the calamity will fall upon the innocent.
They fight over mere grains and ounces, and seek retribution for even a side-long glance. Their entire lives are spent in frowns; a smile upon opening their mouths is rarely encountered.

Throughout their existence, they suffer constant torment; how many instances of satisfaction can there truly be? Even when offices are high and ranks are substantial, honor and disgrace are both met with trepidation. Though granaries overflow and storehouses are piled high, [the mind remains restless].
Gain and loss are particularly grievous; untimely death, illness, decay, and frailty abound. Beings sprout forth in profusion and vanish away in silence.

At the time of casting off this life-span, like a living tortoise slipping from its shell, one gazes in vain at the flesh and bones so difficult to sever, and in empty attachment to the fields and wealth accumulated through suffering.
Evil karma and vengeful enemies pursue one without release; the fetters of habitual afflictions cling to the body and will not depart. This is no ordinary entry [into the next state].

In the fiery cauldrons and the mountains of blades, one is surely destined to be reborn with fur and horns. Therefore, when the Great Awakened One appeared in the world, he called back those lost in the great dream of delusion.

As the holy teachings have been transmitted, the sufferings of this degenerate age may find relief. Opening the Dharma-eye of compassion, he takes pity on the weak who have lost their way at the end of the road.
Once evil deeds have already been committed, how can one extricate oneself from the hells? Only by continuing to cultivate merit and goodness can one hope for deliverance.
To redeem one’s transgressions: as the body falls upon the earth, it rises from the earth; so too, that which is created by the mind must be eliminated by the mind.
To expound the Dharma-gate of repentance is to deliver those submerged in suffering. How fortunate are we, the assembly now performing this ritual of worship, to have prepared for this in advance!

From this moment forth, let us reform our errors and strive for renewal, fearing sin and turning toward goodness. Burning incense and scattering flowers, we set up images and pay homage. May the thousand-year accumulation of darkness be illuminated by a single lamp.
The lamp is used to dispel the profound delusions of ten thousand kalpas. Upon hearing a few words, one attains realization:

the preceding thought clings to objects, while the succeeding thought remains detached; false views are melted away, and right faith becomes firm. Conditioned phenomena and outflows are like flowers in the sky or the moon reflected in water;

the perceiving subject and the perceived object are like echoes in a valley or a city of *gandharvas*. Realizing that the nature of transgressions is fundamentally empty, one enters the meditative concentration of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Thus, my heart...

Ever-mindful. May the Sage’s mirror be ever-bright. I prostrate and pray that [the deceased] may not encounter evil companions, nor meet with evil conditions; may they not utter evil words, nor give rise to evil thoughts.
May their wholesome karma ripen, may their wholesome fruits be perfected, may they practice wholesome dharmas, and may they be guided by virtuous people.

The stars and constellations shall be favorable and flourishing; one's destiny and fortune will be prosperous and unimpeded. During all four seasons, there will be auspiciousness and good fortune; all undertakings and pursuits shall be successfully fulfilled.

One’s mind shall remain steadfast for a hundred years, and health, peace, and blessings shall converge upon their person. Protected by all the heavens, demons and monsters shall remain hidden; they shall not commit the ten habitual transgressions.
By this cause, one shall not receive the retribution of the sixfold entanglements; proceeding directly toward Bodhi, one shall ascend straight to the other shore.

Furthermore, I pray that every person may repent and awaken, that all things may be abundant, and that governance and instruction may bring about transformation. May rain and sunshine be timely and harmonious, free from the calamities of dragon battles, rising *jiao* serpents, mountain collapses, and the crumbling of riverbanks.
May there be no suffering from earthquakes, surging waters, collapsing houses, or sinking ships, and no conflict of war.

May there be no calamities. May there be no fear of famine. May there be no epidemics, plagues, or locusts. May there be no thieves, bandits, or wicked insurgents. May the "Jade Candle" of harmony ever be regulated;
may the "Golden Basin" of the realm remain forever secure. May the myriad regions everywhere enjoy universal compliance and peace. At this time...
The four barbarian tribes followed [these principles] as individuals; each preserved their own domain within the ten wholesome deeds, collectively enjoying peace and stability.

They were not moved by extraordinary objects of desire, nor seduced by those of the night (evil ministers). They did not recklessly exhaust the treasures of Heaven, nor did they dare to violate the will of Heaven.

Retribution was like a shadow following a form or an echo responding to a sound; cause and effect were like the seeds of a gourd or a bean. In principle, there must be repayment; in fact, there can be no discrepancy. All [shared this].
Filled with trepidation, we collectively practice repentance, deeply reflecting upon impermanence, suffering, and emptiness, and aspire to attain the permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
With utmost sincerity, we offer this invocation, beseeching the wisdom-light to bear witness and grant its seal of approval.
Through this verse of confession, one attains Bodhi and subdues Māra;
by proclaiming the names of the Buddhas and the method of repentance, the three thousand Buddhas have arisen thereby. Now, with sincere faith, I make this aspiration.
Based on the *Lengyan Jujing Shisuan* (The Ultimate Repentance Ritual of the Śūraṅgama),
Volume One, composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Chanxiu of Xitansi on Mount Jizu in Nanzhong:
With the utmost sincerity, the great assembly establishes the method of repentance and solemnly purifies the consecrated altar site.
With incense and flowers as offerings, one should give rise to deep and pure faith. Trusting in the Buddha’s words and instructions, first pay homage to the Triple Gem;

thereafter, each person shall state their own intent: from beginningless time until now, the sins of the three karmas and ten evils have been committed, with the six sense faculties acting as intermediaries for thieves, who have plundered the treasures within our own homes.
The master of the five aggregates is deluded, Flowing along with the stream of false imaginings; Falsely grasping at various sensory objects, One falsely enters the six realms of existence.
Knowing that these are false, one should immediately depart from them; When illusion is left behind, true awakening is perfected.
If one must repent and reform, One should contemplate that the nature of sin is empty. If you wish to perform repentance:
Sitting upright, contemplate the true mark, Like the sun illuminating the void.
Like a lamp lighting a dark room, one sees the *dharmadhātu* of *tathatā*, Pure and free from defilement.
From now until the furthest future, together with all sentient beings, May we all attain the pure and white Dharma, And swiftly accomplish the path of Bodhi.
To begin the *Lengyan Jujing Chanfa* (The Ultimate Repentance Method of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra), prostrate with single-minded devotion:

Namo to all the Buddhas who eternally abide like an infinite Indra’s net, throughout the entirety of empty space and the pervasive Dharma-realm, in every atom and every land of the ten directions and three periods of time.
(Chant once and prostrate; the same for subsequent verses.)

Homage to the eternally abiding Dharma, which is as inexhaustible as space, pervades the entire Dharma-realm, and extends through the net of Indra across all lands and moments within the ten directions and the three periods of time.

Homage to that which is as inexhaustible as space, pervades the entire Dharma-realm, and extends through the net of Indra across all lands and moments within the ten directions and the three periods of time.
In the "Chapter on Vows and Practices" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the eternally abiding Saṃgha, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra addressed Sudhana, saying:

"Good son, regarding what is called 'the confession and removal of karmic obstructions,' a bodhisattva reflects to himself: 'Throughout the beginningless kalpas of the past, due to greed, hatred, and delusion, I have [committed...']"

Through my body, speech, and mind, I have committed immeasurable and boundless evil karmas. If these evil karmas possessed a physical form or characteristics, even the entirety of the realm of empty space could not contain them.

Now, with my three karmas purified, I sincerely repent before all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout every atom-sized land pervading the entire Dharma-realm; henceforth, I shall never create them again. Constantly...

Abiding in pure precepts, all such merits shall likewise endure until the exhaustion of the realm of empty space, the exhaustion of the realm of sentient beings, the exhaustion of the karma of sentient beings, and the exhaustion of the afflictions of sentient beings—only then would my repentance come to an end.

Yet, since the realm of empty space and even the afflictions of sentient beings are inexhaustible, this repentance of mine is without end. It continues from moment to moment in succession, without interruption.
There is no weariness or fatigue in the actions of body, speech, and mind. As the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-bhaiṣajyasamudgata-sūtra* states, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed the great assembly, saying:
"In the past, during countless kalpas ago, at the time of the final dharma of the Buddha Prabhāsa..."
Having left the household life to study the Way, they heard the names of these fifty-three Buddhas and their hearts were filled with joy.

They further taught others, and through successive transmission and retention, the number reached three thousand people. By virtue of reverently bowing to these Buddhas, they transcended the sins of birth and death for countless billions of kalpas.
The first thousand people [attained rebirth] during the time of the Buddhas from Flower-Light (*Puṣyarāja*) to Viśvabhū in the past *Vyūha* (Adornment) kalpa.
In this *kalpa*, one thousand people will become Buddhas, from Krakucchanda Buddha to Ruci Buddha, attaining Buddhahood in succession during the present Bhadrakalpa.
Another thousand people will become Buddhas, from Sūryaprabha Buddha to Merudhvaja Buddha, attaining Buddhahood during the Nakṣatra-kalpa.
The Buddha told Ratnākara: "The Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions, such as the Tathāgata Śubhavyūha and others, likewise..."

By virtue of hearing these names of the Buddhas, each shall attain Buddhahood. If there are sentient beings who wish to eliminate the offenses of the four grave prohibitions, who wish to repent for the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds, or who wish to eliminate the extremely heavy offense of groundless slander of the Dharma, they should diligently pay homage to the names of the fifty-three Buddhas.
The *Sūtra of the Three Aggregates* states: "When the various Buddhas dwell in the world..."

Please regard me with compassion. Whether in this life or in previous lives, throughout the beginningless cycle of birth and death, whatever various transgressions I have committed—whether committed by myself, incited others to commit, or rejoiced in seeing them committed;

whether regarding a stūpa or the Saṅgha, or the property of the Saṅgha from the four quarters, whether taken by myself or incited others to take, or rejoiced in seeing it taken; or the five crimes of immediate retribution committed by myself...

Whether one commits them oneself, causes others to commit them, or rejoices upon seeing them committed—regarding the ten unwholesome paths of action, whether performed by oneself, caused to be performed by others, or seen being performed with approval—all such karmic obstructions of sin, whether concealed or unconcealed, lead to rebirth in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals;
or in other miserable destinies, in the borderlands, among the low-born, or as mlecchas. In such places as these...
I now repent for all [transgressions]. May all roots of goodness be dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Those present here in this assembly—monks and laypeople, faithful sons and daughters of noble family—who revere and follow the holy teachings, have given rise to profound and pure faith and together resolved their minds upon *bodhicitta*.
Having established images and performed the ritual procedures, they cultivate and practice the dharma-gate of repentance, contemplating with clarity the truth of non-arising and *nirvāṇa*.
The Sūtra says: "There are two types of brave men: the first does not commit offenses; the second, having committed them, is able to repent. Yet we have long remained on the level of ordinary beings;
every thought that arises, every mental impulse, and every movement of body or speech has been nothing but transgression. How could we possibly refrain from such acts?

It is only because our delusions have accumulated and our evils have matured, because we are deeply habituated and thickly stained by them, that we lack a courageous and resolute mind and do not know how to reform. This is why we revolve [in saṃsāra].
Transmigrating through the six realms, there is no means by which one may extricate oneself. What good fortune it is that we have now encountered the Dharma of Repentance;
this is precisely the time when, having committed [transgressions], one is able to repent. In Sanskrit, *kṣamā* means "requesting forbearance," and is also translated as "repenting of errors.

Speaking in this context, one realizes that one has incurred offenses against the Triple Gem, the devas and nāgas, parents, teachers and elders, and those of seniority within the same altar; one should then earnestly request their forbearance.
May you grant me broad forbearance and compassionately explain [my transgressions]. Pardon my offenses and accept my repentance.
As for all that I have done myself and must now receive—the loss of life and wealth, the clear plotting of conspiracies, and the unfathomable deception—I am truly deserving of these crimes.

I shall vigilantly restrain my thoughts, lash the six sense faculties, give rise to the seven types of mind, repent of the three obstacles, and cultivate a sense of shame and remorse to overcome [them].
Blame oneself and reflect inwardly; feel deep pain and apply oneself to reform and repentance. Vow with determination to seek renewal and never commit such acts again.

Through this single thought of awakening and clear awareness of resentment and affliction, one rides upon the power of the Triple Gem to instantly cause all prior transgressions to dissipate like mist and melt away like ice. Resentment is resolved and enmity is released;
each gives rise to wholesome thoughts and together proceeds to the place of practice (*dōjō*). First, one repents of the ten types [of offenses] that accord with the mind of birth and death.
These are the factors to be remedied: first, the arising of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) based on the false conceptualization of a personal self;

second, the intensification of the "self-centered mind" due to internal possession of afflictions and external encounter with adverse conditions; third, the lack of joy in the virtues of others because one’s own virtuous deeds have been extinguished, both internally and externally;

fourth, the commission of no evil deed whatsoever through the unrestrained indulgence of the three karmas; fifth, the pervasive presence of an evil mind even when one's actions are not extensive; sixth, the characteristic of the evil mind...

1. Continuously day and night without interruption; 2. Concealing faults and transgressions, unwilling to let others know them; 3. Following the entourage of worldly attachments and acting with arrogance, fearing neither the evil realms;
4. Lacking shame and remorse, having no dread for ordinary beings or sages; 5. Denying cause and effect, becoming an icchantika. From beginningless time, there has been nothing that was not thus.
Now you must turn the mind toward goodness and set out upon the wholesome path, going against the current of birth and death and following the stream of liberation.
The Path to Nirvana: Now consider that through mere rectitude one may become a sage, and through a single moment of awakening from delusion one becomes enlightened.

This is evident in principle and as easy as turning over one’s hand. Each of you should give rise to sincere faith, eliminate thoughts of doubt, and by no means cling to worldly talk to the detriment of your own spiritual nature.
Do not run about searching for your head like a person doubled-over in delusion; do not remain drowsy with eyes open, acting as if already awake.

Those who are intoxicated by the times do so because they are wise men who neglect impermanence; their ambitions are overreaching, and they fail to consider that one must ascend from the low ground or travel far starting from the near.
They merely wish to leap suddenly onto a lofty terrace and transcend the mundane world to reach the ultimate reality, thus passing their entire lives in vain.
Having recognized this error, we shall together practice it with our own bodies and tread it with diligence; the place of treasure is not far away.
Exert yourselves individually. With single-minded devotion, let your actions of body, speech, and mind reach their ultimate goal; know nothing else.
Behold only the majestic marks and signs, the Tathāgata’s entire body radiant with light and his compassionate countenance serene and joyful—neither identical to nor different from your own self.
Pervading all of space. I now prostrate myself with my five limbs touching the ground, offering worship exhaustively and without remainder. The resonance between cause and response intersects;
it is as infallible as the beating of drum and clashing cymbals. For the sake of all sentient beings, I take refuge in the immeasurable and boundless Great Compassionate Father.
(Excerpted from the *Buddhanāmasūtra*, translated by Bodhiruci).

Homage to the One Who Constantly Follows the Buddha’s Teachings. (1,255) The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"The ocean of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) abides eternally; moved by the winds of objective spheres, the various waves of consciousness surge and arise.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "The appropriating consciousness (*ādānavijñāna*) is exceedingly subtle; it contains all seeds."
It is like a torrential stream. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The subtle consciousness of *ādāna* (appropriation) forms a torrential stream through its habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The *Abhidharma Sūtra* states: "Because it gathers and stores all dharmas and all seeds, it is called the *ālayavijñāna*.
O Victorious One, when I reveal this, you will know that the essence of this consciousness is the *tathāgatagarbha*. This is because it receives perfuming and maintains the seeds.
This is the root of birth and death. If one is free from conceptual thought and pure, this is the true sound of nirvana. For suchness, though following conditions, does not arise;
yet through the union of non-arising and arising-and-ceasing, there arises the false perception of the body as the root, the world as the vessel, and all that is good or evil, beautiful or ugly.

Arising from delusions and creating karma, they undergo retribution according to their causes; their *dharmakāya* thus revolves through the five destinies, and for this reason they are called "sentient beings.
Although the mani jewel is not defiled by impurities, it has long been submerged in mud and filth; one must use skillful means to draw it out with a rope.

This is like clarifying turbid water or polishing a mirror, whereby clarity is gradually revealed. Ascending the path of the *vajra*, one universally illuminates the ten directions and accomplishes this great task.

Regarding causes and conditions: do not let them be wasted upon the countenance of a man of integrity. If you achieve liberation through a single moment of resonance and enter awakening by following conditions, there will still remain the seeds and manifestations from beginningless time;
these habitual tendencies must also be purified entirely. Each person should examine themselves and reflect upon their own faults.

You should contemplate that the four external great elements and their derivative matter constitute the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), while the four internal great elements and their derivative matter constitute the body of the sense-faculties (*indriya-kāya*). From the distant kalpas of the past, it has been through the eyes and ears...

The six sense faculties—nose, tongue, body, and mind—and the six sense objects—desire for forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—give rise to consciousness based upon these faculties.

Consciousness is that which is capable of discerning; it is conventionally designated as "mind. This so-called mind is not a lump of red flesh within the body; rather, it is a subtle and wondrous spiritual essence.

It is that which gathers all seeds and gives rise to active manifestations (*pravṛtti*), and because it can permeate and accumulate the seeds of all phenomena, it is able to take objects as its conditions.

Because it deliberates upon its own object, and because it arises from the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) as a mental factor (*caitta*) that is associated with and bound to it, it is called *manasikāra* (attention).

Its nature is to alert the mind toward the focal object, drawing it toward that object; it is contact with the object, the experiencing of the favorable and the unfavorable, the arising of the aspects of joy and sorrow, the grasping of images, the application of designations, and the performance of volitional thought. It is characterized by craving for objects of pleasure and aversion [to those that are not].

Regarding the instruments of suffering: they rely on themselves to be arrogant toward others; they lack clarity and possess no wisdom; they harbor doubt and hesitation regarding the principles of the Truths, like the faction of the Six Groups.
They hold perverted views and calculations, like the practices of the six heretical teachers. Clutching anger and harboring resentment, they pursue affliction and dwell upon evil;

concealing and deceiving themselves, they are constantly plagued by regret and unease. They practice hypocrisy and fraud to delude others, always flatteringly complying with what is untrue, and taking pride in their own minor skills.
They treat others with arrogance; they harm people for the slightest offense. When they hear of another’s prosperity or virtue, it feels as if ten thousand arrows pierce their hearts;

when they see someone performing a righteous deed, it feels as if a single hair has been plucked from their bodies. They do not feel shame for their private transgressions, caring little for modesty or remorse, and having no regard for public judgment.

They rarely feel even a trace of guilt or embarrassment, let alone believing that virtue and achievement constitute the four cardinal points of one's character. Thus, they act wantonly without restraint.

How can one know diligence and caution? They are the three jewels for the Way. To be indolent and lax is to lack discipline; to let the six sense-faculties run wild is to damage and obstruct the three virtues.
Dwelling in a state of dull confusion, one is merely muddied by torpor (*styāna-middha*); accumulating lightness and frivolity, one is especially agitated by restlessness (*auddhatya*).
One's right mindfulness is easily forgotten, while one's unwholesome wisdom flows forth unchecked. Addicted to sleep, the mind finds pleasure in darkness.
Inferior. Delighting in what is not calamity, one nonetheless falls into legal punishment; seeking the coarse and wild, one is hurried by names and words;

examining the subtle and minute, one becomes hidden within thought and intention. Observing objects individually and grasping at them repeatedly—whether with or without an underlying essence, whether as the seeing-part or the perceived-part, whether as the self of phenomena or the self of persons—one clings to a measure that is not erroneous regarding the perceiving subject and the perceived object, as if they were real.

Regarding the attachment to defilement and purity, whether as independent entities or solitary reflections, who can fathom the boundaries of mind and境 (objects)? Whether departing later or arriving first, it is difficult to act as a master over birth and death.
Thus, appearing and disappearing within the three miserable realms and circling through the six paths of existence, what karma has not been created?
What class of being has not been traversed? At times one assumes a massive body like a mountain peak; at other times, one is endowed with a minute form like a mote of dust in a beam of light. Evil...

Virtue is meager, while suffering is long and pleasure is brief. Now, having fortunately obtained this human body, we lose our memory across lifetimes; yet if one were to know their past lives, they would be filled with such dread that they could find no peace.
From this point forward, each of us must carry the reality of impermanence; we do not yet know what face we shall wear in the next life, but we must hope to be superior to our present state.
If you can maintain this resolve, you should urgently change your course. May [this merit] be shared with all sentient beings. If...

Whether as kin or as enemies, whether hidden or manifest, whether subtle or overt—among the four modes of birth and the nine classes of beings, since the inception of consciousness, they have been shrouded by ignorance, entangled by fetters, disordered by afflictions, and obstructed by the aggregates and hindrances.
They construct karmic enmities with physical form that exceed the surging waves of the great ocean; they forge offenses devoid of form whose limits equal the vastness of empty space.
At this juncture, you must thoroughly cleanse yourself from the past and overturn [all attachments], as if cutting hair to the skin or clipping nails that have grown into the flesh.
With utmost sincerity and earnestness, confess your own transgressions before the sacred countenance, saying: "Pitifully receive my repentance; may I be purified all at once."

Together, they prostrated with their five limbs touching the ground, fervently praying and bowing before the Tathāgata, the Great Compassionate Father who knows all of the ten directions and the three periods of time.

This central land where we now dwell is not even a grain of rice within a vast granary; the physical forms we have received in our past lives exceed the drifting of a wild horse across the vast desert.
From this, one knows that the number of Buddhas already perfected is like the number of atoms, and the number of infinitesimal particles is likewise beyond measure.
The Buddhas are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; they exhaust the sands of the Ganges. Before one’s eyes, they do not abide for even a moment;

they shift and flow from thought-moment to thought-moment, arising and ceasing in every *kṣaṇa*. I am still the person of old, yet I am not the person of old who sees. Though my face has not yet wrinkled, it is already wrinkled;
when I touch my own body and reflect upon the past, its obscurity and darkness are truly profound. Alas! I am utterly unaware of the three subtle [evolutions].

The six coarse afflictions—how could they possibly sever the nine grades across the nine stages? Their攀緣 (pān-yuan, grasping at objects) becomes more prolonged; their擾動 (rǎo-dòng, agitation) increases all the more.

Their power is difficult to stem like a pillar against a midstream; they merely drift with the current, rushing eastward. Neither mountains nor rivers are truly perilous; the Way of Heaven is easy to understand.

Yet, like clouds that suddenly rain and then disperse, or colors where crimson turns to white, they feign goodness in the light while harboring evil in the dark; they are right in the face but wrong behind one’s back. They study the *Yin Fu* (Secret Talisman) for manipulation, wielding their fame with reckless abandon.

As for the methods of Su Qin, Zhang Yi, Fan Ju, and Cai Ze; Zou Yan, Le Lüe, Sun Bin, and Wu Qi: they stored the wondrous stratagems of the Marquis of Huai (Kang Ying) and employed the secret schemes of Qu Yu (Xuan).
In their cruelty, none could surpass Bai Qi; in their sadistic ruthlessness, they were no different from Shang Yang. Some feigned benevolence and righteousness to steal fame;
some adorned themselves with loyalty and integrity to usurp the state. Some devoured the weak and preyed upon the flesh of others; some used the many to oppress the few. Or...
They disparage the good and praise the evil; they promote the crooked and set aside the upright. They act contrary to the natural order and violate reason, refusing to accept sound counsel.

Their conduct is perverse and their actions subversive, showing no regard for the teachings of the sages. When they slaughter a city, not a single soul is left behind; when they drain a lake, not even a small fish is spared.

They utterly destroy the clans of those whose people they displace, and once they have usurped another's throne, they ensure that the latter’s ancestral sacrifices are forever cut off. Below, they commit acts of incestuous union with their inferiors.
Superior men distance themselves from the intimate; they do not distinguish between the "claws" and the "plums" out of suspicion.
Yet these [others] constantly roam the streets and alleys of flowers and willows, beneath the beams of temples, willingly becoming men who burn or drown.

Upon carriages or amidst the grass, they become women of illicit passion—those who weep for fish and write for phoenixes, those who divide peaches and cut sleeves. They defile pure grounds and blemish chaste households, slandering the reputation of the famous.

[He] flows [into error]. He falsely fabricates the virtues of the high-minded; he claims to have seen what he has not seen, and says he knows what he does not know. He deceitfully proclaims oaths, yet no one understands a single word of them.
He rewards his own obsessive intentions; his incantations bring no awakening. Moment by moment he harms himself, using profit as a net for profit.

He seeks evilly and seeks excessively, intruding where he has no right and coveting what lies outside his station. Clutching his illness, he refuses to repent, yet continues to indulge in greed and gluttony until the brink of peril.
They fail to awaken to this, yet still hope for a long life. Bound by all manner of affections and stained by every kind of attachment, they perceive smoke and know there is fire;
they see fallen leaves and know it is autumn. What man has not done such things? Who has not passed through them? Amidst the rolling dust of the mundane world, where is the path to transcendence?
Across the vast, dark sea of suffering, there is ultimately no oar for deliverance. It is for this reason that the Great Hero, the Great Awakened One, perceives all and knows all.

Knowing this, you give rise to compassion and exercise pity, delivering beings from suffering and bestowing upon them joy. You demonstrate the teachings to benefit and gladden them, pointing out the rungs of the ladder toward goodness and revealing the swift path for advancing on the Way.

You establish eighty-four thousand Dharma gates to shatter eighty-four thousand afflictions, explaining them exhaustively and in detail, instructing us as if holding our ears and speaking face-to-face.
We have gained some knowledge of these aspirations; our innate goodness is deeply pained [by our own failings].
I repent. To reveal and confess my transgressions is as inevitable as it is difficult to conceal them; one cannot escape one's shadow in broad daylight, nor hide one's form within a mirror.
All roots of karma must be uprooted the moment they are recognized. With a mind cleared of turbidity, I prostrate and take refuge in the Compassionate Father of the four modes of birth.

Indeed, according to the imperial edicts of the Central Court, whether a crime be grave or light, and whether it has already been committed or not yet committed, all are fully pardoned upon encountering an amnesty.
A four-line verse from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra can destroy the hells; the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra serves as a writ of pardon before the hall of King Yama;
and the repentance rites of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra can destroy all sufferings and exhaust all unwholesome karma. Thus we know that the Dharma-gate of repentance is truly a means of crossing over.

It is a life-preserving bag floating upon the ocean and a bright torch that dispels darkness. Those whose understanding is profound and whose insight is penetrating will naturally thirst for it and cherish it within their hearts;

what need is there to wait for further exhortation? You should know that since beginningless time, you have employed various deluded thoughts and acted in a state of inversion, thereby bringing about your own cycle of transmigration.

One does not realize that this mind is lively and agile, transcending objects and emerging from the finger [of pointing]. Yet, one falsely speculates it is within, without, in the sense organs, or in between;

one is muddled regarding emptiness and bound by form, abandoning the fundamental and deluded about the return. This is a false vision of individual karma, turning one's back on awakening to unite with the dust of sensory objects.

Regarding what is perceived and what is illuminated, one establishes similarities and differences, causing agitation and weariness, becoming turbid and forming affliction. Day and night, one thinks and reflects, moment after moment.

It does not cease. Within this state, wholesome thoughts are constantly few while unwholesome thoughts are constantly many. Even before an action is performed, it is secretly confronted and darkly contrived:

by recollecting the good, one receives superior retribution; by contemplating the evil, one sinks into ruin of one’s own accord. How much more so when acting openly and manifestly—how could one then possibly enumerate or point out [the consequences]?
It is because we take our single, perfectly integrated, pure jewel of a mind and, through the weaving of the six senses, allow delusion to form; thus, our vision does not transcend the realm of form.
They are stained by the seductive charms of black and white; their hearing does not transcend sounds. They are deluded by the songs and music of Zheng and Wei;

their smelling does not go beyond fragrances. They are submerged in cosmetics, powders, musk, and sandalwood; their tasting never ceases its pursuit of flavors. They crave the flesh and blood of sea and land; their awakening is never free from tactile contact.
Delighting in what is smooth, supple, and beautiful, they know not to transgress the Dharma. Grasping at worldly knowledge and petty wisdom, they are entangled by their shared karma.

Through union and separation, transformation is accomplished; from form, perception arises. Those who differ in aversion yet agree in affection meet and attract one another; through subtle perceptions, they enter the womb.
In the first seven days, it is called *kalala* (coagulated mucus). In the second seven days, it is called *arbuda* (bubble). In the third seven days, it becomes *peśī* (soft flesh).

In the fourth seven days, it becomes *ghana* (solid flesh). In the fifth seven days, it is termed the stage of *praśākhā* (formation); at this point, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are all produced.

All sentient beings, through sexual desire, establish their very life and nature, becoming bound by the fetters of craving and entangled in conceptualization; thus, parents, children, and grandchildren continue the succession of bloodlines, and their species do not cease.
[He] severed [his ties], yet his greedy defilements did not cease. Regarding the sustenance of body and mouth, he relied upon food and drink;

he was unable to consume simple vegetables, preferring instead the sweet and bland, the fatty, the crisp, the pungent, and the savory. They devoured one another in a cycle of mutual exchange and retribution. Today, the strength of this sheep was weak when it was first born, and it had never before tasted such things.
Yet, having surrendered its own body to be food for others, it is now forcibly taken by them against its will to provide for the kitchen.

To unrighteously seize the body, life, or wealth of others involves both killing and theft; thus one incurs the debt of life and the attachment of material goods, which is why birth and death do not cease.
Affectionate love for beauty is the "fish and water" of the emotions; thus one is bound without rest.

This is the fundamental basis upon which the cycle of saṃsāra and the continuity of karmic results are firmly established. As for the subtle and minor transgressions therein, only the Buddhas [can fully know them].
The Bodhisattvas know all and see all, equaling the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
I pray that they will wash me clean with the water of great compassion and grant me the opportunity to repent. I take refuge in the Compassionate Father who possesses the Ten Powers.

Furthermore, those who repent [should realize that] human existence dwells within impermanence, suffering, and emptiness. The entire world is but a transient sojourn, a mere illusion;
yet, though one's life does not exceed a hundred years, one constantly calculates for a thousand. Clinging to emotional views, one solidifies the mark of self (*ātman*).

For this reason, suffering and affliction are most heavy, and calamities are exceedingly many. Friends wither away without one’s realizing it, and kinsmen pass on without one’s being aware of it. Thus, before—
The mountains and rivers of successive dynasties and the landed estates of antiquity have seen many people pass through; they were merely temporary lodgings.
Now, having briefly acquired this [estate], one treats it as a permanent possession. One suffers from the fear of loss at every turn and exerts every effort to preserve it.

Yet, one fails to realize that the empty space of heaven and earth resides within our own wondrously luminous mind—like a single speck of cloud appearing in vast, pure clarity—and that we are recognizing nothing more than the substance of a fleeting bubble.

Exhausting the reaches of the oceans and seas, the Tathāgata has declared these to be those who are to be pitied. Herein, one should repent and eliminate these various sufferings, which are difficult to enumerate exhaustively;
for now, I shall set forth a few examples from what is recorded in the scriptures—matters that have been heard and seen, clearly manifest and evident.

I look up with reliance upon Your Sacred Mirror to repent for and eliminate [the sins of] those within the Middle Kingdom and the foreign lands of Jambudvīpa who, as sovereigns, delight in killing rather than abstaining from it;
and for the court officials and ministers who, holding their breath and standing on tiptoe, manage to preserve even a single day as if it were ten years of hardship.
I repent for those who, by means of remonstrance, talent, poetry, or prose, have offended against taboos and caused death.

[Repentance for] the suffering of being killed; the suffering of being killed due to the weight of power; the suffering of being killed due to the weight of reputation; and the repentance for and removal of the sins of slandering to death, killing out of envy, false accusation to death, and accidental killing.
[Repentance for] the suffering of being ensnared by cruel officials who, seeking to curry favor with their superiors, engage in fabrications and secret denunciations;

and the suffering of being implicated and exterminated along with one’s entire clan when the virtuous and loyal are summoned or dragged down by the instigation of others. [Repentance for] the mutual slaughter of kinsmen, the succession of wars and resulting calamities, and the factionalism among various princes.
I repent for the suffering of forcibly relocating the imperial carriage and killing people until they filled the city, with blood flowing so thickly it floated the helmets of soldiers;

I repent for the suffering of losing the "stag" [the Mandate of Heaven] in the Central Plains, where weapons were sought daily and the Nine Provinces were split into sixteen kingdoms in a state of war;

I repent for the suffering of powerful ministers who usurped the sovereign, whose authority daily diminished while their confidants and partisans filled the palace court, such that every movement of rising or sitting, or every summons, was met with interference.

[He] repents and eliminates the suffering of restricting access to the classics until they total one hundred, of calculating the addition of the nine emoluments (*jiuxi*), and of transferring the mandate and abdicating the throne;

he vows that in future lives he shall not be born into a royal family but seek instead to be a commoner—a hardship from which it is impossible to escape. He repents and eliminates the suffering of executing and suppressing the eminent and heroic, of imposing lifelong prohibitions upon the brilliant and talented, of banishing the worthy and good, and of demoting those who are the hope of the people.
He repents and eliminates the suffering of the Palace Attendants (*changshi*) and military commanders who, relying on their favor, monopolize power.

I repent for the suffering of the sovereigns of the dark age who killed the upright to vent their wrath upon the world, yet were suddenly overtaken by calamity, facing the agony of near-total extermination through execution;

for the suffering caused by the sale of offices and titles, the rampant practice of bribery, and corrupt officials and sycophantic clerks who perverted the law for personal gain, who were harsh and lacked benevolence, and who drained the people’s marrow while leaving only their bones;
for the suffering of governors whose families were wiped out and magistrates whose households were ruined; and for the prevalence of bandits and thieves. I repent for all these things.
I repent for the suffering of highway robbery and plundering villages, and the kidnapping of people and livestock;

I repent for the removal of violent levies and arbitrary taxes, such as the *jianjia* (household structure) tax and the *keqiang* (money on demand), as well as the suffering of being forced to pay taxes upon entering the market empty-handed;

I repent for the suffering of incessant military campaigns and the transport of supplies filling the roads; and I repent for the conscription of soldiers based on landholdings and the drafting of men by household size, where fathers...

The pain of children being separated from their parents; the cries of estranged husbands and wives; the suffering of becoming a ghost in a foreign land after departing a thousand times without ever returning across barbarian mists and pestilential seas, or through enemy fortresses and desert sands;

the repentance that removes the suffering of traveling by night under the auspices of spirits, the suffering of marching swiftly with silenced mouths, the suffering of losing one's way and falling over cliffs, the suffering of pits without water, the suffering of drinking horse urine, the suffering of fingers falling off in the cold, and the exhaustion of gasping for breath while being driven on.
Suffering. The suffering of lice and nits arising from one's armor; the suffering of two armies facing each other at the lines; the suffering of raiding camps and plundering fortifications;

the suffering of reporting on the enemy and scouting; the suffering of fighting a desperate battle to the death; the suffering of whistling arrows and flying cannons; the suffering of slaughter upon the battlefield;
the suffering of fleeing in defeat; the suffering of being trampled by warhorses; arrows piercing the eyes and metal weapons wounding the body—seeking life, one cannot find it. Seeking...

The suffering of not being able to obtain food until death; the suffering of the siege of a city; the suffering of being surrounded by enemies; the suffering of being unable to purchase three *sheng* of rice with three *jin* of gold;
the exhaustion of eating grass roots and tree bark; the exhaustion of eating leather shoes and woven belts; and the exhaustion of chewing on straw mats.
The suffering of eating raw fur and wool and consuming the flesh of one's own children; the agony of splitting bones for fuel while repenting for the sins of weighing and selling human flesh;
the misery of seeing one’s wife and children dragged away by soldiers to be slaughtered, unable to protect or stop them;
the hardship of being emaciated and exhausted, yet still bearing arms to fight atop city walls; and the longing for reinforcements to arrive, where a single day feels like three autumns passing.
The suffering of the "Full City" (Pūrṇa), where people devour one another until nearly extinct; the suffering of the "Repentance-Expunging" (Kṣapaṇaka), where people are measured by the crowd;

the suffering of the "Flesh-Eaters," where violent men regard human flesh as dried meat (lakhā); the suffering of the "Mortar-Man," where people are placed in mortars; or known as the "Burnt Grasp-Fire," or the "Unpleasant Soup," or the "Two-Legged Sheep," or the "Bitterness of Boiling Bones.
The suffering of the "Repentance-Expunging Corpse-Pile," where rotting corpses accumulate in the wilds, their foul stench熏天 (pervading the heavens). White.
May we repent to eliminate the suffering of being buried in mountainous piles of bones where no one remains;

may we repent to eliminate the suffering of famine and calamitous years following great military conflicts, where epidemics spread so virulently that people fall ill upon merely catching a scent, leaving every household empty;

may we repent to eliminate the suffering of markets overflowing with pearls, jade, and gold while lacking even a peck of grain; may we repent to eliminate the suffering of nine out of ten years of floods and seven out of eight years of drought.

The suffering of drought when the season has passed; the suffering of long-lasting rain that does not clear; the suffering of locusts and swarms of insects covering the heavens and devouring the grain crops;

the suffering of ice, hail, and fierce winds that knock down the ripened fruits and grains; and the suffering of repentance for the destruction of prefectures, counties, villages, and shops by bursting rivers and oceanic tides.
I repent for the suffering of fire and calamity that has spread through villages and neighborhoods, reducing them to ashes and embers;

I repent for the suffering of officials, merchants, and mariners who have encountered whirlwinds and perished in snowy waves; I repent for harboring evil intentions and false views, which sever the roots of goodness and extinguish the nature.
I repent for destroying temples and ruining stupas, mutilating images and fragmenting scriptures—acts that lead to the suffering of falling into hell.

I repent for flogging and torturing monks and nuns, insulting and reviling śramaṇas, mocking the monastic community, and slandering those of pure conduct—deeds that lead to the suffering of entering the evil realms.

I repent for seeing people in hunger and cold yet refusing to provide for them, seeing those begging in the streets yet refusing to give alms, and being stingy and miserly while adding insults to their plight.

One shall fall into the suffering of the hungry ghosts (*preta*). Confess the breaking of the harmony of the Saṃgha, the disparagement of the precepts and discipline, the disruption and dispersal of assemblies for offerings, the obstruction and abandonment of virtuous deeds, and the destruction of the forest of merit—thereby bringing about the suffering of the Avīci Hell.

Confess and eliminate adverse planetary limits (*daśā*), the life-palace (*mūlatrikoṇa*), hostile stars and malefic luminaries, the mutual overcoming of the five elements (*pañcabhūta*), the states of decline, illness, death, and the tomb, as well as the annual *vadhaka* (killer), monthly calamities, and [adverse] days and times.

[May there be] the removal of the afflictions of *xingchong* (clashing and opposing), *guanfú* (official seal), *jì'ài* (sickness and calamity), *tàisuì* (the year star), *yīnfǔ* (the underworld), *zāituì* (disaster and retreat), *kōngwáng* (void and loss), and being obstructed by *dàhào* (great expenditure).

[May there be] the removal of the suffering caused by the four seasonal pathogenic influences and the decline of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), as well as the removal of chronic and stubborn ailments that cause one to lie long upon the bed and mat, and the suffering of failing to recover despite medical treatment.
[May there be] the removal of strange diseases and monstrous sores, where skin and bone stand bare together, with pus and blood dripping profusely, foul and putrid.

The suffering of being difficult to approach; the confession and removal [of sins] for those who are sojourning in lodgings as travelers, or wandering as guests at the ends of the earth. Their gold in the bags is exhausted, and their sable furs are worn through.

Having no door through which to seek audience, they lack the means to sustain themselves. Having lost their way in the clouds and mists, they are cut off from those who can provide them with patronage.
The suffering of being destitute in a foreign land and unable to return to one’s hometown;

the suffering of scholars traveling for study and monks wandering on pilgrimage, left alone like a solitary shadow in cold temples and desolate villages, beset by illness and groaning in pain, with no medicine or medical care and no relatives or friends to look after them—may these be expiated through repentance.
May the sufferings of smallpox, of a short lifespan, and of poverty be expiated through repentance.

The suffering of poverty; the suffering of low birth; the suffering of blindness and deafness; the suffering of being mute and dumb; the suffering of incomplete physical form; the suffering of having withered hands and feet or being lame;

the suffering of being one-eyed or short-statured; the suffering of cold and the suffering of heat; the suffering of hunger and the suffering of thirst; the suffering of lacking coarse clothing and inadequate food and drink;

the suffering of repenting and expiating violations of the law; the suffering of encountering legal punishment; the suffering of banishment and exile; the suffering of imprisonment; and the suffering of repenting and expiating for pregnancy.

The suffering of illness; the suffering of miscarriage; the suffering of difficult labor; the suffering of birth complications; the suffering of being unable to deliver the infant; the suffering of the placenta failing to descend;

and the suffering of those who, having served in the inner palace, long for the Emperor's favor; those who dwell in resentment within the household, longing for their husbands; those whose marriages are delayed; and the suffering of widowers, widows, orphans, and the solitary.

I repent for and eliminate the suffering of being castrated by others; the suffering of self-castration; the suffering of suicide by hanging; the suffering of suicide by cutting one's own throat; the suffering of suicide by ingesting poison;
and the suffering of leaping from precipices or falling into wells. I repent for and eliminate the suffering of enemies administering poison; the suffering of assassins stabbing one.

I repent for and eliminate the suffering of being mangled and bitten by tigers and leopards; the suffering of being stung by snakes and scorpions. I repent for and eliminate [the suffering of] earth, stones, mountains, cliffs, pits, hollows, and mounds.

High and low, uneven; thorns, poisonous herbs, and the suffering of being filled with filth and impurity—may all such harms and agonies experienced by the human world, both the environment and its inhabitants, be entirely eliminated through the power of the Triple Gem from this day forward, so that they shall never again be encountered or endured.
I pay homage to the Great Compassionate Father.

The Sūtra says: From beginningless time until this very day, we have failed to recognize the Buddhas and the kindness of our parents;

we have not understood wholesome dharmas and have committed manifold evils. Relying on our own lineage and various wealth and treasures, we were dissolute in our prime and committed all manner of [transgressions].
They engage in evil conduct; their thoughts are unwholesome, and they commit evil deeds with their speech. Following whatever their minds dictate, they fail to see their own faults.

Such is the foolish behavior of ordinary worldlings, shrouded in the darkness of ignorance. Associating with evil friends, their minds are distracted by afflictions. Due to the conditions of the five desires, anger arises in their hearts.
Lacking knowledge of contentment, they intentionally commit various evils. Associating with those who are not noble, they give rise to stinginess and envy, resulting in poverty.
Due to causes and conditions, they commit evil through deceit and flattery; bound to others, they are constantly filled with fear and lack self-mastery as they create various evils.
Greed, hatred, and delusion agitate their minds; driven by craving, they commit manifold evils.
Depending on clothing, food, and the beauty of women, they produce various afflictions and fevers, thereby committing manifold evils. Thus, they accumulate the evils of body, speech, and mind.
Regarding the three types of karma: whether one has lacked reverence for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; whether, due to a lack of wisdom, one has slandered the True Dharma;

or whether one has failed to show respect to parents and elders, being shrouded by delusion and ignorance, arrogant and heedless—the extremely heavy evil karma committed throughout a thousand kalpas shall all be completely extinguished through sincere repentance.
May the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who possess great compassion, bear witness to this.

With sincere sincerity, I mournfully accept my repentance. If, due to the various evils I have committed over a hundred kalpas, I am born into great sorrow and suffering, poverty and destitution, anxiety, feverish distress, and alarm;
if I fear my evil karma and my mind is constantly debased, finding no moment of joy anywhere;
then for all the defilements and impurities that I possess, I pray that the Buddhas of the present—
World-Honored One, wash away and purify [these transgressions] with the water of great compassion. All past evils are now confessed;

for the sins committed in the present, I sincerely arouse a transformative resolve. Regarding those not yet committed, I dare not do them again. As for the sins already committed, I dare not conceal them.
For the retribution received from the three types of bodily karma, the four of verbal karma, and the three of mental karma—the perils of the six realms—I offer this sincere confession.

I repent. May I distance myself from the ten unwholesome actions, practice the ten wholesome actions, and abide securely in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). May I attain the state of the Honored One of Ten Powers (*daśabala*).
For myself and all sentient beings whose faculties are impaired, may they all be made complete; for those emaciated by the suffering of illness, may they all be liberated.

Whether one suffers flogging, imprisonment, shackles, or fetters; whether one is distressed, fearful, or has a mind agitated by sorrow; or when facing execution—may there be no measureless [suffering].
They shall be completely liberated from all fears, sufferings, and afflictions. The hungry shall obtain fine food; the thirsty shall obtain sweet drink.
The blind shall regain their sight; the deaf shall regain their hearing; the mute shall be able to speak; the naked shall obtain clothing.

Those who are impoverished shall immediately find a treasure trove, their storehouses overflowing so that they lack for nothing. Sentient beings shall look upon one another with harmonious countenances and joyful expressions. Others...
These are virtuous deeds; I rejoice in them and praise their fulfillment. May all women become men, endowed with wisdom and diligence, practicing the path of the Bodhisattva.

May all unpleasant karmic retributions be utterly extinguished. May they tear asunder the net of craving and shatter the prison of the three realms of existence, attaining Great Nirvana and abiding in peace and bliss of body and mind.
Having finished this repentance and making these vows, I take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem.

Next, we again perform repentance for the eight sufferings of the human realm. These are called the sufferings that serve as the basis for all other suffering:

the suffering of birth—where ignorance moistens karma and one undergoes impure conception, which then grows and emerges from the womb; and [the suffering of] noble and lowly, male and female, the handsome and the ugly. Furthermore, it can...

That which causes transformation and decay is called "aging. Suffering arises as each moment passes away, eventually leading to total destruction; one’s strength cannot pull it back, and there is nothing but lamentation.
Furthermore, the disharmony of the four great elements is called the suffering of illness; the body is then oppressed by the four hundred and four diseases.

When the mind is not at peace, one becomes sorrowful and distressed; the攀緣 (pān-yuan, objects of attachment) fly about and leap across without ceasing. Furthermore, it can extinguish the various faculties (indriya); this is called the suffering of death.
Although the seasons change and pass away, or when adverse conditions are summoned, or when karmic retribution suddenly arrives, even if one possesses merit, there is no life.

When one’s merit is exhausted, it is difficult to survive. There are nine kinds of violent and untimely deaths. Furthermore, being forced to dwell together with immeasurable external conditions that are not beloved is called the suffering of association with the hated (*apriyasaṃprayoga-duḥkha*).
Enemies and foes act as relatives and friends, plotting and harming one another; they create rifts and harbor resentment, causing the mind to experience painful states.
Good intentions do not result in favorable conditions; moreover, what is dear is met with opposition, which is called the suffering of separation from the beloved (*priyaviprayoga-duḥkha*).

To be separated from what one loves: a compassionate parent, a filial child, a doting wife, a tender infant, or a brother as dear as a twin—objects that delight the mind and gladden the heart—suddenly encounters impermanence.

In an instant, they are parted; the liver and belly are shattered, and the pain pierces to the very marrow of the bones. One must bear this grief while performing the funeral rites, with no hope of meeting again.
Furthermore, when one’s hopes are not fulfilled, it is called the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks. When poor, one seeks wealth; when destitute, one seeks...

One may attain worldly success: long maintain one's desires, swiftly achieve one's wicked ambitions, bring fame to oneself, and bind upon oneself noble titles. One repeatedly acquires rare objects and possesses unique treasures;

fields extend across the roads and valleys, with cattle and horses measured by the grain they consume. Yet, despite exerting effort in calculation and management, things go contrary to the heart and violate one's plans;

unable to achieve one's aims, one blames heaven and accuses others. Furthermore, when all these various sufferings are taken together, it is called the "blazing intensity of the five aggregates" (*pañca-skandha-paridāha*).
Suffering can shroud the mind; as it accumulates and binds within the various realms of experience, one cannot clearly perceive them.
It causes a searing fever that carves away one's nature and destroys its authenticity. Yet, the cause of all suffering is rooted in lustful desire. As the Sutra in Forty-two Sections states:

Fortunately, there is one [point]: it is truly the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*), the very root of the ruin of the Way. One must understand that both one’s own body and the bodies of others consist of five kinds of impurity:
First is impurity of the place of birth: this body is foul and filthy; it does not arise from a lotus flower. Second is impurity of the seed:
the seed of this body is impure, arising from the perverse conceptions of the father and mother. Third is impurity of intrinsic nature: the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)...
1. An impure accumulation: the ocean water cannot wash away its uncleanness. 2. Impurity by its own characteristic: it constantly flows with impurities, like a bag filled with filth.
3. Ultimate impurity: when one contemplates this body with discernment, it will ultimately return to the place of death.
Though one may observe its makeup, its radiant beauty, its vivid smiles, and its clever charms, it is nothing but a cavity full of pus and blood, bloated, foul, and loathsome—a skeleton.
It is a state of utter disorder. The wise practice non-action, yet those who are submerged in溺愛 (溺愛, *ni'ài*—溺愛, "sinking love" or "excessive attachment") sink into the mud.

If one can lighten and thin this [attachment] by even a single part, it is the shortcut to rebirth in heaven. Through this, the merit of Chan wisdom increases. Birth is truly suffering, a confluence of great calamities.
Having realized this, let us together repent and eliminate [these faults], and reverently pay homage to the Great Compassionate Father.

Within the body, the elements of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion are divided into seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing. From beginning to end, these five layers become turbid and muddled, like earth thrown into water;
their appearance is thus. When emptiness and the perception of forms interweave, it is called the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (the age of turbulence). This refers to the faculty of the body.

Mutual striking is called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). The mutual conditioning of faculties and objects is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). The mutual pursuit of delusions and karma is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).
The divergence of nature and function is called the turbidity of life-span (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*). Dividing into faculties and consciousnesses, the clarity adheres and gives rise to nature;

the six [sense-faculties] act as thieves' intermediaries, plundering the family treasure. Through the accumulated empty habits of successive lives, there arise the phases of birth, abiding, change, and extinction, along with their respective measures and numbers, flowing forth in wild abandon.
Rushing and galloping; light and dark, motion and stillness; penetration and obstruction, tranquility and change;

separation and union, arising and ceasing—these twelve conditioned characteristics are ultimately identical within the midst of difference. Once the six knots have been formed, right and wrong arise like sharp spikes.

The nature of the mind becomes frantic and chaotic, and false perceptions erupt. As these delusions do not cease, the wearying faculty of sight gives rise to the dust of defilement. If the eyes are fatigued, one sees phantom flowers.
Chaos arises; mountains, rivers, the great earth, birth and death, and all inversions are but frantic toil.

Not knowing how to untie the knot, how can one hope for even a single moment of cessation at the very heart of the knot? To eliminate its dusty appearances without yet understanding the matter at hand is merely to abandon worldly toil while following the current, drifting away to drown.
This violates the three determinations, contradicts the Great Meaning, and ruins the person of the City of Nirvana. [End of] Section.

The mind is called precept (*śīla*). Once the impulse for lust stirs, the mind cannot be restrained; the dust of passion cannot be cleared away. One falls into the pit of craving and false views, losing the path to Bodhi.
It is like steaming sand to make rice—the cause and effect do not correspond. Furthermore, a compassionate heart is called precept.
Once the impulse for killing arises, injury and harm will surely be manifold; evil cannot be halted. Beyond the three-inch tip of the tongue, one fills [the hells] for a lifetime.

In these mountain streams and ravines, the seeds of Buddha-nature are severed and the roots of karma for the three miserable realms grow long. Enemies and creditors lie in wait to pursue one at every opportunity;
the vast ocean of suffering is difficult to cross by any means. To flee drowning only to leap into fire is an act that ought not to be done.

Furthermore, contentment is called precept (*śīla*); yet once the intent to steal lies hidden, the thieving mind erupts. To harbor deceit is to violate righteousness; seeking to delude oneself and others leads to utter extinction.
In sincerity, one who has lost a spouse may be pure and good, yet through expedient means they steal incantations.

They steal the property of others, as well as the belongings of spirits and ghosts, or the goods of thieves—even a single needle or a blade of grass—seeking thereby to extinguish their sins. This is like pouring water into a leaking cup. Furthermore, truthful speech is called a precept;
yet we commoners, lacking the authoritative testimony of the sages, often speak lies and frequently commit falsehoods, desiring only to appear superior to ourselves.
Thus, there is no good that does not return to him. If he wishes to suppress others who are inferior, there is no evil that he will not encounter.
Even if one were to carve human excrement into sandalwood, it would never reach its true fragrance; once the *tāla* tree is cut down by a blade, its roots of goodness are forever destroyed.

His mouth is the source of the most grievous of all sins, and thus he suffers the most intensely. Furthermore, he has violated the four *pārājika* dharmas of a bhikṣu, which are the thirteenth [category of grave offenses].
The Saṃghāvaśeṣa dharmas, the two Aniyata dharmas, the thirty Naiḥsargika-pāyattika dharmas,
the ninety Pāyattika dharmas, the four Pratideśanīya dharmas, the one hundred Śaikṣa dharmas, and the seven Adhikaraṇa-śamatha dharmas;
as well as for the bhikṣuṇīs, the eight Pārājika dharmas, the seventeen Saṃghāvaśeṣa dharmas, the two Aniyata dharmas, and the two [Pāyattikas].
The one hundred and eight *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas, the eight *pratideśanīya* dharmas, the one hundred *saṃvara* dharmas,
and the seven methods for settling disputes; furthermore, the violation of the ten grave *pārājika* precepts and the forty-eight minor stains of the Bodhisattva *prātimokṣa*,
extending even to the three thousand majestic deportments and eighty thousand subtle practices, as well as the ten [precepts] of a *śrāmaṇera*.
The laymen and laywomen who observe the five precepts have neither conscious intent nor ignorance; thus, regarding transgressions committed through negligence or error, they together repent.
For past faults, they purify them again and regain the precepts; for future offenses, they resolve not to continue them, severing and eliminating them forever.
They take refuge in the Unsurpassed, Greatly Compassionate, Two-Legged World-Honored One, praying that he grant the witness and seal of his merit.

"The wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and marks. Originally it does not exist; worlds and sentient beings arise due to delusion."
There is birth. Because of birth, there is cessation. From ultimate non-existence, one attains ultimate existence.

This existence and its contents have no causal basis, no abiding place, and no defining characteristics; they are utterly without root. Based on this non-abiding, the world and all sentient beings are established.
Being deluded regarding the original perfect luminosity, this gives rise to false imagination. Perfumed by this, karma is formed. Through the mutual resonance of shared karma, existence comes to be.
Sentient beings are subject to inversion. There is existence because there is grasping; through the false arising of fragmented segments, they dwell where there is no dwelling.

Because they flow and shift without staying, there is the inversion of the world. The three periods of time and the four directions intermingle and harmonize, transforming sentient beings into twelve categories.
When the mind moves, there is sound; when the mind arises, there is form. These six disordered delusions exhaust the twelve transformations into one.
They revolve through birth from eggs, birth from wombs, birth from moisture, and spontaneous birth; through forms and formlessness; through perception and non-perception;
or that which is neither with form nor without form, neither with perception nor without perception. Due to the eighty-four thousand afflictions, they undergo transformations and distinctions.
Together we repent within this world of flux and the realms of segmented existence, riding upon this world.

The realms arise through the mutual production of karma and its fruits. Because of the movement of false, deluded saṃsāra, the combination of vital energies (*vāyu*) forms eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts of flying and sinking;
thus there exist egg-born beings (*aṇḍaja*), such as the *kalala* stage, which emerge from shells and circulate through various lands.

Fish, birds, tortoises, and snakes fill these categories. Through the repentance for karmic retribution, one seeks to purify the defilements of the world and the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). Desire...
Due to inversion, they combine and flourish into eighty-four thousand horizontal and vertical disordered thoughts;

thus there arise the classes of beings such as those born from a womb, from an egg, from moisture, or by transformation—humans, animals, dragons, seers, and so forth. Through the repentance of karmic retribution for attachment to the cycle of rebirth and the pursuit of inversion, they combine with warmth to form existence;
thus there arise eighty-four thousand overturned and disordered thoughts, and hence there is the stage of moisture (*saṃsveda*).
The corpse, relying on moisture, gives rise to wriggling and crawling creatures such as woodworms, mosquitoes, and gadflies;

through the repentance for karmic retribution, these undergo transformation within the cycle of rebirth due to the influence of delusion. Through the union of contact, eighty-four thousand new and old chaotic thoughts arise;

thus there exist transformed forms and *kalala* (embryonic stages) that emerge suddenly where none existed before—such as metamorphosing insects, birds, frogs, pheasants, and clams. [Karmic] transgressions...

Informing the assembly that they should all know this retribution, may they receive it according to their own thoughts; filled with trepidation and alarm, they take refuge in the Great Compassionate Father who possesses the five eyes, the six supernormal powers, the three clarities, and the eight liberations.
